title: Cache strategies: cache-aside, write-through, write-back
summary: Choose how data moves between your application, the cache and the database on reads and writes.

values.aside: App checks the cache, loads from the database on a miss and fills the cache
values.through: Reads hit a cache that is kept current by writes
values.back: Reads hit the cache, which may hold newer data than the database

values.aside: Write to the database, then invalidate or update the cache entry
values.through: Write to the cache and the database together, synchronously
values.back: Write to the cache and flush to the database later

values.aside: Brief staleness between write and invalidation

values.back: Data not yet flushed is lost if the cache fails
High: batching, ordering and failure handling

aside: Read-heavy data where occasional staleness is acceptable.
You want a simple default that survives cache failures.
through: Reads must see recent writes and consistency matters.
back: Write-heavy workloads where you can accept a small loss window.
You can buffer and batch updates safely.

watchOut: Cache stampede when a hot key expires: coalesce requests or jitter TTLs.
Invalidation is the hard part: define who owns it before you add the cache.

title: Vertical vs horizontal scaling
summary: Decide whether to make one machine bigger or add more machines.

values.vertical: Bigger CPU, memory and disk on one machine
values.horizontal: More machines behind a load balancer or partitioning scheme

values.vertical: Hardware limits and rising price per unit of capacity
values.horizontal: Much higher, limited by coordination overhead

values.vertical: Single point of failure unless replicated
values.horizontal: Survives losing nodes if designed for it
Stateless services, shared state outside instances, data partitioning
More moving parts: deployment, service discovery, monitoring

vertical: You are early and load fits one machine comfortably.
Simplicity matters more than headroom right now.
horizontal: You need fault tolerance or growth beyond one machine.
Workload splits cleanly across independent requests or partitions.

watchOut: Scaling out stateful services without a plan for session and data locality.
Premature distribution: a single well-tuned node often takes you surprisingly far.

title: Layer 4 vs layer 7 load balancing
summary: Choose whether the load balancer routes on connection details or understands the application protocol.

values.l7: Route by URL, host or header; canary and A/B routing

values.l4: Very fast and cheap: no payload inspection
values.l7: More CPU and latency per request
Often terminates TLS to inspect and route
Caching, compression, auth, rate limiting, request rewriting

l4: You need maximum throughput or non-HTTP protocols.
Simple distribution across identical backends is enough.
l7: You route by path or host, or run several services behind one address.
You want the balancer to enforce auth or rate limits.

watchOut: A single load balancer is itself a single point of failure: run redundant pairs.
Sticky sessions hide state in the balancer: prefer stateless services.

title: Rate limiting: fixed window, sliding window, token bucket
summary: Choose an algorithm by how it treats bursts, accuracy and memory.

values.fixed: Count requests per fixed time interval
values.sliding: Weight the previous window's count by how much it overlaps the current one
values.bucket: Tokens refill at a steady rate; each request spends one

values.fixed: A burst of up to twice the limit can straddle a window boundary
values.bucket: Allows bursts up to the bucket size, then the steady rate
A token count and a timestamp

fixed: A rough limit is enough and simplicity wins.
sliding: You want a smooth limit without storing every request time.
Boundary bursts would hurt a backend.
bucket: Short bursts are fine but the average rate must be bounded.
You want intuitive burst and rate parameters.

watchOut: Read-then-write counters race across servers: use atomic operations.
Decide fail-open or fail-closed for when the limiter store is down.

title: News feed: fan-out on write vs on read
summary: Choose whether to precompute each user's feed when a post is created or assemble it when the feed is requested.

values.write: At post time: copy the post id into each follower's feed
values.read: At read time: gather recent posts from everyone the user follows

values.write: Very low: the feed is ready
values.read: Higher: many lookups and a merge

values.write: High for users with many followers

write: Most users follow a moderate number of accounts and reads vastly outnumber posts.
Feed read latency is the top priority.
read: A few accounts have huge audiences, so push would be too expensive.
Storage and write amplification must stay small.

watchOut: The celebrity problem: use a hybrid that pushes for normal accounts and pulls for very large ones.
Offset pagination breaks on a moving feed: use cursors.
